## Transformer-layer distillation: TinyBERT An encoder can give the correct class label while representing the sentence differently from its teacher. TinyBERT supervises intermediate computations as well as the final prediction. Both networks read the same tokenized input; the student fits selected embedding, hidden-state and attention tensors. This is encoder compression, not SFT on generated chains of reasoning. The objectives are described in [Jiao et al., §3.1–3.2](https://aclanthology.org/2020.findings-emnlp.372.pdf#page=3) and the [official implementation](https://github.com/huawei-noah/Pretrained-Language-Model/tree/0598f02d7fc4eaa7b4cbc1e9d7ab18bc875c24f9/TinyBERT). ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/distillation-tinybert-2026-11-05/tinybert-layer-detail.png|TinyBERT: attention-score and hidden-state matching between teacher and student layers]] *Xiaoqi Jiao et al., [TinyBERT, Figure 2](https://aclanthology.org/2020.findings-emnlp.372.pdf#page=3). Complete author-supplied [layer-detail PNG](https://arxiv.org/html/1909.10351v5/transformer_layer_detail.png), unchanged. The upper comparison fits attention scores; the lower one fits hidden states after projecting the student's width. The published ACL illustration is covered by [CC BY 4.0](https://aclanthology.org/faq/copyright/).* ### Which layers and tensors are compared For a four-layer student and a twelve-layer teacher, the paper uses $g(m)=3m$: student layers 1, 2, 3 and 4 match teacher layers 3, 6, 9 and 12. The embedding output is a separate match at index 0. The four-layer model has hidden width 312 rather than 768, but both networks have twelve attention heads. Their per-head score matrices therefore have the same $L\times L$ shape for an input of length $L$, even though their head dimensions differ. These sizes and the layer mapping are specified in [the model settings, §4.2](https://aclanthology.org/2020.findings-emnlp.372.pdf#page=5). For a matched layer, the paper defines $$ \begin{aligned} L_{\mathrm{attn}} &=\frac1h\sum_{i=1}^{h} \operatorname{MSE}(A_i^S,A_i^T),\\ L_{\mathrm{hidn}} &=\operatorname{MSE}(H^S W_h,H^T). \end{aligned} $$ Here $H^S$ has shape $L\times312$, $H^T$ has shape $L\times768$, and $W_h$ maps 312 coordinates to 768. Embeddings use an analogous projection. The teacher is fixed; gradients update the student and its projection. The classification output can be trained against the teacher's class distribution using soft cross-entropy. These targets constrain different tensors; matching one does not establish that the others match. ### Attention scores are not attention probabilities TinyBERT's $A=QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$ is the matrix before softmax. Adding a constant to every entry in one row leaves its attention probabilities unchanged, but changes the score-matching loss. For example, take two rows $(0,1)$ and $(2,0)$, then add 5 to the first and subtract 3 from the second. The resulting probabilities are identical. The mean squared score difference is $$ L_{\mathrm{attn}}=\frac{25+25+9+9}{4}=17. $$ Its gradient with respect to the four student scores is $(2.5,2.5,-1.5,-1.5)$, so this loss still changes the student. It imposes a stronger condition than matching softmax probabilities. The paper reports better convergence for its score-based target; the arithmetic above explains the difference between objectives, not a universal advantage. The pinned training loop replaces scores at or below $-100$ with zero before MSE, removing large masking sentinels. This threshold does not inspect a separate validity mask: an unmasked score below it would also be zeroed. The loop then averages over the resulting tensor, including those zeroed cells. Padding can therefore change the denominator. In the same example, padding both matrices to $4\times4$ and zeroing masked cells reduces the global mean from 17 to 4.25; the mean over the original valid pairs remains 17. ```python tinybert_teacher_scores = torch.tensor( [[[[0., 1.], [2., 0.]]]], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True) tinybert_row_offsets = torch.tensor([[[[5.], [-3.]]]], dtype=torch.float64) tinybert_student_scores = ( tinybert_teacher_scores.detach() + tinybert_row_offsets).requires_grad_() tinybert_score_loss = F.mse_loss( tinybert_student_scores, tinybert_teacher_scores.detach()) tinybert_score_loss.backward() tinybert_same_probabilities = torch.allclose( tinybert_student_scores.softmax(-1), tinybert_teacher_scores.detach().softmax(-1)) tinybert_padded_s = F.pad( tinybert_student_scores.detach(), (0, 2, 0, 2), value=-10000.) tinybert_padded_t = F.pad( tinybert_teacher_scores.detach(), (0, 2, 0, 2), value=-10000.) tinybert_padded_s = torch.where( tinybert_padded_s <= -100, 0., tinybert_padded_s) tinybert_padded_t = torch.where( tinybert_padded_t <= -100, 0., tinybert_padded_t) tinybert_padded_loss = F.mse_loss(tinybert_padded_s, tinybert_padded_t) assert tinybert_teacher_scores.grad is None print("same probabilities:", tinybert_same_probabilities) print("score MSE:", tinybert_score_loss.item()) print("score gradient:", tinybert_student_scores.grad.tolist()) print("padded global MSE:", tinybert_padded_loss.item()) ``` This is a tensor calculation, not a TinyBERT training run. It uses one head and two valid tokens, without a tokenizer or dataset. The actual [loss branch](https://github.com/huawei-noah/Pretrained-Language-Model/blob/0598f02d7fc4eaa7b4cbc1e9d7ab18bc875c24f9/TinyBERT/task_distill.py#L935-L976) also fixes the layer correspondence. Its zero-based attention indices are $2,5,8,11$, whereas the representation list includes embeddings and selects $0,3,6,9,12$. Confusing these lists introduces an off-by-one layer match. The [student class](https://github.com/huawei-noah/Pretrained-Language-Model/blob/0598f02d7fc4eaa7b4cbc1e9d7ab18bc875c24f9/TinyBERT/transformer/modeling.py#L1119-L1142) shares one `fit_dense` projection across its embedding and layer outputs; `nn.Linear` includes a bias. Do not infer one independently trained projection per layer from the paper's compact notation. The classification helper also uses `.mean()` over classes as well as examples. For $C$ classes this adds a factor $1/C$ relative to the usual class-summed soft cross-entropy; a new implementation must choose its normalization explicitly. ### General and task-specific distillation ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/distillation-tinybert-2026-11-05/tinybert-overview.png|TinyBERT: general distillation followed by task-specific distillation on augmented data]] *Xiaoqi Jiao et al., [TinyBERT, Figure 1](https://aclanthology.org/2020.findings-emnlp.372.pdf#page=2). [Complete original PNG](https://github.com/huawei-noah/Pretrained-Language-Model/blob/0598f02d7fc4eaa7b4cbc1e9d7ab18bc875c24f9/TinyBERT/tinybert_overview.png); no redraw, crop or translation. CC BY 4.0 for the published ACL illustration.* The first stage uses a pretrained, not task-fine-tuned, BERT teacher on a general text corpus. It trains intermediate representations and embeddings, without prediction-layer distillation. The resulting student initializes the task-specific stage. Here the teacher is a BERT already fine-tuned for that task. The task data are augmented using BERT word predictions for single-piece words and GloVe neighbors for multi-piece words. The official recipe first fits intermediate tensors, then runs prediction distillation with `--pred_distill`. The paper's combined notation does not mean every loss is active in every training phase. [The original README](https://github.com/huawei-noah/Pretrained-Language-Model/blob/0598f02d7fc4eaa7b4cbc1e9d7ab18bc875c24f9/TinyBERT/README.md) documents that sequence. These encoder experiments use sentence-level tasks; they do not establish transfer of autoregressive reasoning or identical internal algorithms. A reduced student still needs evaluation on the intended tasks, with the tokenizer, layer mapping and loss reductions recorded.
